lessons.title: Files That Remember: Creating, Checking, and Deleting with the File Class

objectives.cognitive: Explain what a File object represents and distinguish between naming a file and creating it on the disk.
objectives.affective: Value careful record keeping by checking what a method returns before assuming a file was created or deleted.
objectives.psychomotor: Write and run a program that creates a file and a folder, lists the folder, and deletes a file, checking each returned value.

blocks.markdown:
**Where we left off:** your folder should already have `Vehicle.java`, `Jeepney.java`, `Tricycle.java`, `Bus.java`, `OverloadException.java`, `InvalidDistanceException.java`, and `VehicleNotFoundException.java`. None of them change this week. Save a copy of `Main.java` as `Main_week14.txt`.

**The problem this week fixes:** last week your fleet lived in an `ArrayList`. When the program ended, the list disappeared. A program that must **remember** needs to save its data in a **file**.

**No internet needed.** Keep every class in its own file, all in one folder. The text files you make this week go in the same folder. Compile with `javac *.java`, run with `java Main`.

A program creating, reading, writing, and deleting files on the computer's disk, so data stays after the program ends. Java's tools for this are in the `java.io` package (io = input and output). A **text file** holds plain characters you can open in Notepad.

The barangay hall keeps records in a **filing cabinet**. Writing a label "Fleet records" on an index card does **not** put a folder in the cabinet: that is a `File` object. Someone still has to make the folder (**create**), look inside it (**read**), add pages (**write**), or throw it out (**delete**). The cabinet keeps the folder even after the clerk goes home, just like a file stays after your program ends.

rows: names a file or folder; creates, checks, lists, and deletes it
read a text file one character, or one whole line, at a time
read words and numbers from a file; read a String as if it were a file
write to a file (replace it, or add to the end); build text in memory

blocks.instruction: Replace `Main.java` with this, then run it **once**. A File object is only a name, until you create it.

File name: fleet.txt
Exists before? false
Created now? true
Exists after? true
Is a file? true
Size in bytes: 0
blocks.checkYourself: Run Step 1 a **second** time. Predict first: what will `Exists before?` and `Created now?` say? (The file is already there, so `createNewFile()` refuses and returns **false**. It does not erase the file.)

activity.instruction: Create fleet.txt twice in the same run. Immediately after printing Created now, call createNewFile() again and print "Created again? " followed by its boolean result. Start in a clean exercise folder.
activity.expectedOutput:
File name: fleet.txt
Exists before? false
Created now? true
Created again? false
Exists after? true
Is a file? true
Size in bytes: 0

blocks.markdown: **Look closely:** `new File("fleet.txt")` did not make a file: `exists()` said **false**. Only `createNewFile()` made the real (empty) file, so its size is **0 bytes**. Keep `fleet.txt`; you will fill it on Tuesday. `createNewFile()` can throw an `IOException`, a **checked** exception from Week 13, which is why it sits inside `try`.

blocks.markdown: **Words to know this week.** **Path**: where a file is; a plain name like `fleet.txt` means "in the folder where you run `java Main`." **Read**: bring data from a file into the program. **Write**: send data from the program into a file. **Overwrite**: erase the file and write it fresh. **Append**: add to the end and keep what was there. **Close**: tell Java you are done with a file, so everything is saved and the file is released.
A `File` can also name a **folder** (also called a directory). `new File(folder, "trips.txt")` means "trips.txt inside that folder."

blocks.expectedOutput:
Folder made? true
Is a folder? true
Inside records: [old_log.txt, trips.txt]
Delete old_log.txt? true
Delete it again? false
Delete the folder? false
Left inside: [trips.txt]
blocks.checkYourself: Run Step 2 again. Now `Folder made?` says **false** (the folder already exists) and the list shows `old_log.txt` again, because `createNewFile()` made it again. Why does `Arrays.sort(names)` come before printing? (`list()` promises no order, so sorting makes everyone's output match.)

activity.instruction: After deleting old_log.txt twice, delete trips.txt and print "Delete trips.txt? " plus the result. Then run the existing folder deletion and listing. Print an empty array if folder.list() is null because the folder was deleted. Start with a clean records folder.
activity.expectedOutput:
Folder made? true
Is a folder? true
Inside records: [old_log.txt, trips.txt]
Delete old_log.txt? true
Delete it again? false
Delete trips.txt? true
Delete the folder? true
Left inside: []

blocks.markdown: **Read it carefully:** the second `delete()` gave **false**: there was nothing left to delete. The folder also refused to be deleted: Java only deletes a folder when it is **empty**, and `trips.txt` is still inside. These methods **return false** instead of throwing an exception, so always check what they return.

questions.prompt: What is a `File` object? Does `new File("fleet.txt")` create the file on the disk? How do you know (Step 1)?
In Step 1, `createNewFile()` gave **true** on the first run and **false** on the second. Why?
In Step 2, `folder.delete()` gave **false**. Why? How is "returning false" different from throwing an exception like Week 13's `OverloadException`?

lessons.title: Line by Line: Reading Text Files with FileReader and BufferedReader

objectives.cognitive: Describe how FileReader and BufferedReader read a text file, and what readLine() returns at the end of a file.
objectives.affective: Show patience and accuracy when typing data files, recognizing that one wrong character can stop a program.
objectives.psychomotor: Type fleet.txt and write a program that loads it with BufferedReader into an ArrayList of Vehicle objects.

blocks.markdown: An object that brings characters **from** a source into your program. `FileReader` reads a text file **one character at a time**. `BufferedReader` wraps around another reader and adds `readLine()`, which reads a **whole line** at once and gives `null` when there are no more lines.

The dispatcher reads the terminal logbook to the drivers. `FileReader` is like spelling it out letter by letter: "N... X... A...", correct but slow and tiring. `BufferedReader` is like reading one full line of the logbook at a time: "Jeepney, NXA 123, Mang Ramon." When she reaches the last line, there is nothing more to read: that is `null`.

**New: try-with-resources.** A file you open must be **closed** when you are done. If you write `try (FileReader reader = new FileReader(...)) { ... }`, Java closes it for you at the end, even if an exception happens.

blocks.instruction:
**Step 3a:** open `fleet.txt` (made in Step 1) in **Notepad**. Type the four lines shown in `fleet.txt` **exactly**: commas, no spaces after commas. Save it.

**Step 3:** replace `Main.java`. This reads the file one character at a time.
blocks.expectedOutput:

blocks.markdown: `read()` gives each character as a **number** (its code), and **-1** at the end of the file. That is a lot of work just to get one line.

blocks.markdown: **Look closely:** `toVehicle()` returns a `Jeepney`, a `Tricycle`, or a `Bus`, but its return type is `Vehicle`. That is **polymorphism** from the Four Pillars. `split(",")` cuts a line at every comma into an array; `Integer.parseInt("50")` turns the text "50" into the number 50.

questions.prompt: What does `readLine()` give back, and what does it give back when the file has no more lines?
Why do we open the reader inside `try ( ... )` (try-with-resources)? What does Java do for us at the end?
Write the class or method that does each job: a) reads one character; b) reads one whole line; c) turns "50" into 50; d) cuts a line at every comma.
In Step 4, `toVehicle()` returns a Jeepney, Tricycle, or Bus, but its return type is `Vehicle`. Which Week 12 idea is this, and why is it useful here?

lessons.title: Count the Fares: Reading Files with Scanner and StringReader

objectives.cognitive: Compare reading a file with Scanner and with BufferedReader, and explain what StringReader is for.
objectives.affective: Practice honesty with data by stopping safely at bad input instead of adding wrong numbers to a total.
objectives.psychomotor: Write a program that totals fares from fares.txt with Scanner, and a method that reads from both a StringReader and a FileReader.

blocks.markdown: You already know `Scanner` from reading the keyboard (`new Scanner(System.in)`). Give it a `File` instead, `new Scanner(new File("fares.txt"))`, and it reads the file word by word and **number by number**. `hasNextDouble()` looks ahead and answers "is the next word a number?" without using it up.

At the end of the day, the canteen cashier runs her finger along the price list and adds up only the **numbers**, skipping spaces and new lines. Before adding, she checks: "Is this a number?" If she hits a word like "abc," she stops instead of adding nonsense. That cashier is `Scanner` with `hasNextDouble()`.

blocks.instruction:
**Step 5a:** in Notepad, make a new file `fares.txt` in the same folder, with the two lines shown (sample fares, not real LTFRB rates).

**Step 5:** replace `Main.java`.
blocks.expectedOutput:
Fares read: 5
Total collected: P89.0
Average fare: P17.80
blocks.checkYourself: Change `fares.txt` to `13.00 15.00 abc` on line 1 and run. Now `Fares read: 2`: `hasNextDouble()` said "not a number" at `abc`, so the loop stopped safely. If you call `nextDouble()` without asking first, it crashes with `InputMismatchException`. Put the file back.

activity.instruction: Keep fares.txt unchanged. Read each number, then count and add it only when the fare is at least P15.00. Compute the average from the accepted fares.
activity.expectedOutput:
Fares read: 3
Total collected: P63.0
Average fare: P21.00

blocks.markdown: A reader whose source is a **String** in memory, not a file on disk. Because `FileReader` and `StringReader` are **both** kinds of `Reader`, one method can read from either.

Before reading the real class record, a teacher practises on a **photocopy** of two sample rows. Same reading method, safer source. `StringReader` is that photocopy: you can test your reading code without touching the real file.

lessons.title: Overwrite or Append? Writing Files with FileWriter, BufferedWriter, and StringWriter

objectives.cognitive: Differentiate overwriting from appending a file, and explain why every writer must be closed.
objectives.affective: Show responsibility for other people's records by choosing append when history must be kept, and overwrite only when it may be replaced.
objectives.psychomotor: Write programs that overwrite and append a log file, save and reload the fleet with BufferedWriter, and build a report with StringWriter.

blocks.markdown: A writer sends characters **from** your program **to** a destination. `new FileWriter("trip_log.txt")` **overwrites**: it erases the file and starts it fresh. `new FileWriter("trip_log.txt", true)` **appends**: it keeps what is there and adds to the end. If the file does not exist yet, both make it.

The terminal has a **whiteboard** for "Next jeepney to leave": each new note erases the old one (**overwrite**). It also has a **logbook** where every departure is a new line under the last one (**append**). Choose the wrong one and either the logbook loses its history or the whiteboard fills up with old news.

blocks.instruction: Replace `Main.java`. `showFile()` prints a file so you can see inside it; you will reuse it.

activity.instruction: Change only the second FileWriter to append mode. Keep both original write calls. The first trip must survive the second write.
activity.expectedOutput:
--- trip_log.txt ---
NXA 123 left Monumento
TRC 456 left Bagong Silang

blocks.markdown: **Only one line!** The second `FileWriter` erased the NXA 123 line. That is overwrite mode.

blocks.instruction: Keep `showFile()` from Step 7. Replace only the `main` method (the whole file is shown here). Append mode: the logbook grows.
blocks.expectedOutput:
--- trip_log.txt ---
TRC 456 left Bagong Silang
BUS 789 left Caloocan
NYB 321 left Sangandaan
blocks.checkYourself: Run Step 8 again. Predict: how many lines now? (Five: append never erases, so the two new lines are added again.)

activity.instruction: Begin with the original Step 7 log containing the Tricycle line. Change Step 8 from append mode to overwrite mode. Keep its two write calls; the old Tricycle line must disappear.
activity.expectedOutput:
--- trip_log.txt ---
BUS 789 left Caloocan
NYB 321 left Sangandaan

blocks.markdown: Wraps around a `FileWriter` and collects text in memory, then writes it in big pieces, which is faster for many lines. `newLine()` ends a line the right way for each computer (Windows and Linux end lines differently). Its text reaches the file only when the writer is **closed**, so always use try-with-resources.

A writer whose destination is a **String in memory**, not a file. You write into it piece by piece, then `toString()` gives you all the text at once: to show on screen, save to a file, or both.
The dispatcher drafts the daily report on **scratch paper** first, then reads it aloud and copies the same text into the record book. `StringWriter` is the scratch paper.

rows.fix: Make every line complete, e.g. Jeepney,NXA 999,Mang Jun,Recto.

lessons.title: Programs That Remember: File Handling Performance Task and Presentation

objectives.cognitive: Justify the choice of reading and writing classes, and of overwrite or append, in their own file-based program.
objectives.affective: Show respect for classmates' work by testing each other's programs fairly and giving helpful feedback during presentations.
objectives.psychomotor: Build, test four ways, and present a program that loads, saves, appends to a log, and reports its own data without crashing.

blocks.markdown: Today you finish and present the **Performance Task**: make your own program remember its data. Run it four ways before you present, then answer the Friday exit slip.

questions.prompt: Name your data file and your log file. Write what one line of your data file looks like, and the method that turns it into an object.
You used overwrite for one file and append for another. Defend both choices. What would go wrong if you swapped them?

The school clinic wants a program that keeps (a) the list of learners with their LRN and section, and (b) a record of every visit, including the time. Which of this week's classes would you use for each, and would each file overwrite or append? Why?
Compare your program last week, which forgot everything when it ended, with this week's. What can it do now that it could not do before? What part was hardest?

performanceTask.title: Performance Task: Make Your Program Remember
performanceTask.markdown:
Open your own program from last week's Performance Task (your sari-sari store, pets, gadgets, school personnel, or shapes theme). Make it **save** its data to a text file and **load** it back the next time it runs. Start on Thursday after the Thursday exit slip; finish and present on Friday.

**Reuse this week's code.** Your `toObject` works like `toVehicle()` (Step 4). Your `toLine` works like `toLine()` (Step 9). Use `showFile()` (Step 7) to check what your files hold.

**A good order for main:** 1) check and load the data file, 2) make the changes, 3) append to the log, 4) save the data file, 5) build and save the report.

**Example (sari-sari store), first run with the given stock.txt:**

- Skipped bad line: Rice (kg),fifty
- Stock saved: {Bread=8, Softdrink=24}

**Testing tip:** run your program at least four ways: (1) normally; (2) a second time: the log must grow, the data must not double; (3) with the data file renamed: a polite "no data" message; (4) with a bad line added: that line is skipped. Every run must end normally, never with an `Exception in thread "main"` report.

**Plan before you type** (show your teacher): for your data file, log file, and report file, write the file name, what one line looks like, and whether it is overwritten or appended, and why.
checklist: A data file with one object per line (at least 4 lines, at least 2 subclasses)
exists() checks the data file first; if it is missing, say so politely
Load with BufferedReader + readLine() into your List
A toObject / toLine pair: text to object, object to text
Save the List back with BufferedWriter and newLine() (overwrite)
Append one line to a log file each run: new FileWriter(name, true)
Build a short report with StringWriter; show it and save it
A bad line is skipped with a message (NumberFormatException), never a crash
Every reader and writer is inside try-with-resources
Make a temporary file, then delete() it and print the result
A comment on each part, e.g. // APPEND: keep old log lines
presentationOutline: Introduce your theme and your files: data, log, report. (30 sec)
Run it: show the data loading and the report. (1 min)
Prove it live: run again and open the log in Notepad; rename the data file; add a bad line. (2 min)
Point to the code for load, save, and append, and say why. (1 min)
questionsToPrepare: Why overwrite for the data file but append for the log?
What does your program do if the data file is missing?
What does try-with-resources do for you?
When would Scanner be better than BufferedReader?
Why does your toObject method return the parent class?

rubric.criterion: Load: at least 4 objects from 2+ subclasses load from the data file with BufferedReader; text becomes objects.
Save: the List is saved back with BufferedWriter and newLine(); running twice does not double the data.
Log + report: the log grows by appending; a StringWriter report is shown and saved.
File class: exists() is checked before loading; a temporary file is created and deleted.
Error handling: missing file and bad line give friendly messages; try-with-resources everywhere; no crash.
Presentation and Q&A: proves each part live; explains overwrite vs. append and every choice with own code.
